title: Project Overview
description: Travel Life is a full-stack travel documentation app for tracking trips, locations, photos, transportation, lodging, and journal entries. The README lays out the tech stack — a React/TypeScript frontend and an Express/TypeScript backend backed by PostgreSQL with PostGIS via Prisma — and the Docker-based development workflow that ties them together. Keep this stack in mind as the tour moves from the two application entry points down through each architectural layer.

title: Backend Entry Point
description: backend/src/index.ts is where the Express server comes alive: it wires up CORS, security headers, CSRF protection, and rate limiting, mounts every API route, exposes Swagger docs, serves protected static files, schedules cron jobs, and handles graceful shutdown. As the highest-scored entry-point candidate in the dependency graph, it is the root from which nearly the entire backend can be reached — everything in the next few steps is something this file pulls in, directly or indirectly.

title: Frontend Entry Point
description: On the client side, frontend/src/main.tsx is the mirror image of backend/src/index.ts: it mounts the React application into the DOM and imports the global stylesheet. From here, App.tsx takes over — establishing routing, initializing authentication state, wiring up global error handling, and rendering the app-wide layout (Navbar, MobileBottomNav) that every page sits inside.

title: Backend Foundations: Errors, Middleware, Database
description: Before looking at any single feature, it helps to see the shared plumbing every backend route depends on. errors.ts defines the AppError class used throughout the codebase for consistent HTTP error responses (the single highest fan-in file in the whole project, at 50 incoming references). auth.ts is the JWT-verifying middleware that guards protected routes, checking a token blacklist and a password-version cache for instant session invalidation. database.ts configures the Prisma connection with a retrying startup health check. Together these three files are the backbone that the Backend API and Service layers build on.

title: Backend Layered Architecture: Routes -> Controllers -> Services
description: The backend follows a strict layered architecture: Routes define URL/method mappings, Controllers parse and validate requests, and Services hold the actual business logic that talks to Prisma. trip.controller.ts handles trip CRUD, duplication, and health checks, delegating the real work to trip.service.ts. This routes -> controllers -> services -> Prisma -> database chain, documented in BACKEND_ARCHITECTURE.md, repeats for every resource in the app (locations, photos, activities, and more).

title: Frontend Architecture: Pages -> Services -> Stores
description: The frontend mirrors the backend's layered discipline: Pages compose Components, which call Services to talk to the API, while Zustand Stores hold global client state. TripDetailPage.tsx is the largest and most central page, hosting tabs for locations, activities, lodging, transportation, journal, and albums. axios.ts (the frontend's single highest fan-in file, referenced 57 times) configures the shared Axios instance — including the response interceptor that unwraps the backend's `{status, data}` envelope — while authStore.ts manages login/session state with Zustand. FRONTEND_ARCHITECTURE.md documents this pattern in full.

title: Core Domain Types
description: Both frontend and backend lean heavily on a shared vocabulary of TypeScript types. trip.ts, location.ts, and photo.ts are among the highest fan-in files in the frontend (34, 34, and 35 references respectively), meaning nearly every component and service that touches a trip, location, or photo imports these definitions. These types establish the contract between the UI layer built in Step 6 and the API responses coming from the backend layer built in Step 5.

title: Cross-Cutting Feature: Entity Linking
description: Entity Linking is a generic system that connects any two trip entities (a photo to a location, a journal entry to an activity, and so on) rather than hard-coding each relationship individually. entityLink.service.ts on the backend creates, verifies, and cleans up orphaned links, backed by entityLink.types.ts's Zod schemas; entityLink.service.ts on the frontend and the useEntityLinkSync hook keep the UI's linked-entity state in sync after creates and updates. This pattern shows how the layered architecture from Steps 5-6 supports a feature that cuts across every entity type in the app.

title: Cross-Cutting Feature: Offline / PWA Support
description: Travel Life is a Progressive Web App: offlineDb.ts wraps IndexedDB (via the idb library) to define an offline schema mirroring the server's entities, offline.service.ts caches trips and manages a pending-changes sync queue for when connectivity returns, and offlineDownload.service.ts orchestrates downloading an entire trip — including map tiles — for offline use. manifest.json declares the installable PWA shell (icons, theme, shortcuts). This subsystem depends on the same type definitions from Step 7 to keep offline and online data shapes consistent.

title: Cross-Cutting Feature: PDF / AI Import
description: The PDF import pipeline lets users upload a travel itinerary PDF and have an LLM extract structured trip entities automatically. pdfImport.service.ts on the backend handles upload and background AI-assisted parsing into pending entities awaiting review, exposed through pdfImport.routes.ts; aiSuggestion.service.ts separately powers AI-driven entity-link suggestions using GPS proximity, temporal overlap, and name matching. On the frontend, usePdfImportPolling.ts polls the import status until it reaches a terminal state, giving users live feedback during the AI extraction process.

title: Data Layer: Prisma Schema and Migrations
description: schema.prisma is the single source of truth for the database, defining all 32 models (User, Trip, Location, Photo, Activity, Transportation, Lodging, EntityLink, and more) with PostGIS-backed geospatial fields — this is what the trip.service.ts and entityLink.service.ts from earlier steps ultimately read and write through the Prisma client. The 20260103_add_postgis_coordinates migration shows the schema evolving in practice, adding geography(Point,4326) columns and GIST spatial indexes to locations and photos for efficient geospatial queries. DATABASE_SCHEMA.md documents the full model set and relationships.

title: Infrastructure: Containerization
description: Both services ship with multi-stage Dockerfiles. backend/Dockerfile.prod compiles the TypeScript app and generates the Prisma client in a builder stage, then produces a minimal Node 20 Alpine runtime image running as a non-root user with a migration-aware entrypoint. frontend/Dockerfile.prod builds the Vite/React bundle in a Node builder stage and serves the static output from an nginx Alpine image. docker-compose.yml ties both services together with PostGIS and a self-hosted Nominatim geocoding service for local development.
languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use multiple FROM statements: a builder stage installs dev dependencies and compiles the app, while the final stage copies only the compiled artifacts into a minimal runtime image. This keeps production images small and avoids shipping build tools, source maps, or dev dependencies to production.

title: Infrastructure: CI/CD and Deployment
description: The docker-build-test.yml GitHub Actions workflow builds and tests both Docker images on every push and pull request, catching containerization breakage before it merges. release.yml automates the release process itself, building and publishing versioned images and tagging releases. Together with the docker-compose.prod.yml and TrueNAS-specific compose variants seen in Step 12, this is the full path from a code change to a running production deployment, as detailed in the project's BUILD_AND_PUSH.md release process.
languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows are triggered by `on` events (push, pull_request), organize work into `jobs` that can run in parallel, and execute sequential `steps` within each job. Caching dependencies between runs and gating merges on required checks are common patterns for keeping CI fast and reliable.
